g.text: One material, three jobs: keeping out the cold together with a CO₂ layer, stopping radiation, and carrying its own weight.

text.style: font-weight: 700; font-size: 15px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #111111
font-weight: 700; font-size: 15px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #111111
font-weight: 700; font-size: 15px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #111111

g.text: Ice is not a good insulator.
Its conductivity is ±2.9 W/m·K at −60 °C, about the same as granite.
The real insulator is the layer of CO₂ cells (±0.01 W/m·K). The cell
walls carry a metal film so heat cannot leak out as radiation.
it keeps the habitat warm and keeps the ice cold.
Warmer ice creeps faster (see 3). Target: R ≥ 4 m²K/W.
the day–night temperature swing reaches only ±23 cm into the ice,
so the interior does not follow the outside cycle.
Ice is rich in hydrogen. Light hydrogen nuclei slow particles down
without shattering them into many secondary particles, unlike
Dose on the Martian surface: ±0.64 mSv/day
(±230 mSv/year, measured by the Curiosity rover). A 0.6 m ice shell
= ±55 g/cm², plus ±20 g/cm² of atmosphere. Most solar particle
storms are stopped; galactic cosmic rays are reduced gradually.
clear ice transmits daylight. Freezing from the bottom up
pushes bubbles out, so the ice does not turn cloudy.
Strong in compression, weak in tension.
Cold ice crushes above ±5 MPa in compression but cracks at ±1 MPa
in tension. A catenary shape keeps the arch in compression only:
46 kPa (16 m span) to 92 kPa (32 m), over 50× below crushing.
Ice under load for years flows slowly, like a glacier. Every
20 °C warmer makes creep 10–20× faster. So the ice is kept
≤ −50 °C, and larger spans need thicker ice.
0.6 m for 16–24 m spans · 1.25 m for a 32 m span
Sources: Hassler et al. 2014 (Science, Curiosity RAD); Cuffey & Paterson 2010 (ice creep); Petrenko & Whitworth 1999 (ice properties); team calculations (structural integrity appendix).
